screens.title: Particle Filter Localization
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why particle filters exist, how they represent belief with particles, and when they outperform classic Gaussian estimators. We start from the practical problem: a robot that does not know where it is, or that sees ambiguous places that produce two or more plausible locations. Kalman-style filters assume a single Gaussian hypothesis and will collapse multimodal possibilities into one average that is often wrong. Particle filters solve this by representing the full distribution with many sampled hypotheses called particles. You will see the three core algorithmic moves: prediction using a motion model plus noise, update using sensor likelihoods, and resampling to focus computation on plausible areas. I will also highlight failure modes — degeneracy and impoverishment — and common practical fixes like adaptive resampling and random particle injection for kidnapped-robot recovery. By the end you will understand when to choose a particle filter, the basic MATLAB structure for implementing Monte Carlo Localization, and the concrete visualization you can use to debug and teach this approach.

screens.title: Why Kalman Filters Fail for Global Localization
screens.narratorSegment: Begin by clarifying a common misconception: Kalman filters are not wrong, they are specialized. A Kalman filter represents the robot state as a single Gaussian distribution. That is ideal when motion and measurement noise are approximately Gaussian and the posterior remains unimodal. But many realistic localization problems are multimodal or non-Gaussian. For example, at startup the robot's pose prior is uniform; the robot could be anywhere on the map. Later, ambiguous environments create multiple equally plausible poses — two identical corridors produce a bimodal posterior. A Kalman filter collapses these modes into a single average, which often sits between the true hypotheses and produces meaningless estimates. Particle filters, by contrast, represent the full posterior with samples and naturally express multimodality. A key practical check is to visualize the belief: if your distribution has separated clusters, a sampling approach is required. Remember a common trap: adding process noise to an EKF does not create multiple peaks. It only broadens a single mode. The takeaway is clear: use Kalman methods for well-localized, approximately Gaussian scenarios and use particle methods when the belief can split or when sensors produce non-Gaussian uncertainty.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.3 › Why Kalman Filters Fail
Concept

Unimodal Gaussian vs multimodal reality

Kalman-style estimators represent belief with a single Gaussian. That works for small uncertainties around one hypothesis. When belief splits, a single Gaussian is misleading.

Concrete example
Two identical corridors produce two separate high-probability clusters. An EKF would return the mean between them, which lies in free space but is not a true hypothesis.
Common misconception
Adding noise to an EKF does not create multiple peaks; it only widens the single Gaussian. Multimodality requires nonparametric or mixture representations.
Key Takeaway

If your posterior can split, use a sampled representation like a particle filter rather than a single-Gaussian estimator.

Contrast visual
Particles show separate hypotheses. The purple ellipse is a single Gaussian which cannot capture both clusters simultaneously.

screens.title: Particles as Hypotheses
screens.narratorSegment: A particle is simply a sampled hypothesis of the robot's full state, typically pose in 2D: x, y, and heading. Collectively, particles form a non-parametric approximation to the posterior distribution. The key idea is density: regions with many particles represent high posterior probability. This representation is flexible: it handles uniform priors, multimodal posteriors, and arbitrary noise models. Practically, implement particles as a list of structs or arrays with fields for pose and weight. Sampling uniformly across free space creates a uniform prior. As the robot moves and senses, particles migrate and reweight, forming clusters around likely locations. An important practical point is memory and compute scaling: the number of particles needed typically grows with state complexity, and each particle may require an expensive sensor prediction such as ray casting. Visual inspection is an invaluable debugging tool: plot particles as blue dots, and show the weighted mean as an estimate. Also compute diagnostic statistics such as variance and effective particle number. A useful heuristic is to begin with a few hundred to a few thousand particles and adjust based on map complexity and available C P U. What matters is that the particle set remains diverse enough to represent plausible alternatives.

Representation

Particles approximate the posterior by sampling

Each particle stores a pose and a weight. Together they approximate any distribution shape without assuming parametric form.

screens.title: Prediction Step (Motion Update)
screens.narratorSegment: The prediction step moves each particle according to the robot's motion model plus process noise. This models uncertainty in control and odometry. Implementing this is straightforward conceptually: add the commanded displacement to each particle's pose and then add random noise sampled from the motion noise distribution. In MATLAB, a loop over particles updates x, y, and theta by delta values plus noise terms drawn per particle. Important practical notes: apply motion in the particle's local frame if the motion model is odometry-based, and ensure angular wrapping for theta. Use vectorized operations when possible to speed up MATLAB code. Too little motion noise will prevent particles from covering the true posterior after uncertain moves; too much noise will scatter particles and reduce weight concentration. For example, if odometry sigma is 0.1 meters per step, sample additive Gaussian noise per particle with that sigma. Finally, keep the prediction code separate from the sensor update to simplify testing and debugging. Prediction Step (Motion Update) means move particles with the motion model and add realistic process noise; vectorize updates for performance.. In practical terms, propagating particles with the motion model and process noise. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.3 › Prediction Step
Motion update

Propagate particles with odometry and noise

Apply the commanded displacement to each particle and add sampled noise using the motion noise parameters. Keep frame conventions consistent.

MATLAB-style loop (illustrative)
for i = 1:num_particles
    particles(i).x = particles(i).x + delta_x + noise_x;
    particles(i).y = particles(i).y + delta_y + noise_y;
    particles(i).theta = particles(i).theta + delta_theta + noise_theta;
end
Vectorize this update when possible to improve performance in MATLAB.
Example
With odometry sigma = 0.1 m, sample per-particle Gaussian noise to reflect uncertain wheel slip.
Common mistake
Applying noise in the world frame when the motion is expressed in the robot frame. This misplaces predicted particles.
Why this matters

The prediction step spreads particles according to control uncertainty. It maintains hypotheses that the update step can later confirm or discard. Tuning noise controls exploration vs. concentration trade-offs.

Key Takeaway

Motion update should reflect real odometry noise and use consistent frame conventions to preserve meaningful hypotheses.

screens.title: Update Step (Sensor Likelihoods)
screens.narratorSegment: The update step weights each particle by the likelihood of the observed sensor measurement given the particle's pose. For range sensors, compute expected ranges using ray casting from the particle pose into the known map. Then evaluate a Gaussian likelihood for each beam: the closer the expected range to the observed range, the higher the likelihood. Multiply beam likelihoods to get the particle weight, or sum log-likelihoods to avoid numerical underflow. Practical tips: normalize weights to sum to one, clamp extremely small weights, and use log-space for many beams. If your sensor has non-Gaussian characteristics, adapt the likelihood model accordingly. A common optimization is to subsample beams or precompute ray-cast tables for faster expected-range queries. Also watch for correlated beams: multiplying many nearly redundant likelihoods can overconstrain the weights. After updating, inspect the weight distribution: if nearly all weight is on a few particles, degeneracy is imminent and resampling may be required. Finally, remember to keep weights non-negative and reset them after resampling. Update Step (Sensor Likelihoods) means weight particles by sensor likelihoods derived from expected measurements; normalize and monitor weight concentration to detect degeneracy.. In practical terms, compute how well each particle explains the sensor observation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.3 › Update Step
Sensor update

Compute particle weights from sensor likelihoods

Use ray casting to predict expected ranges, then evaluate a likelihood function for each beam and combine them into a particle weight.

MATLAB-style update (illustrative)
for i = 1:num_particles
    expected = ray_cast(particles(i), map);
    weight = 1;
    for j = 1:num_beams
        weight = weight * gaussian_likelihood(z(j), expected(j), sigma);
    end
    particles(i).weight = weight;
end
Use log-likelihoods and normalization for numerical stability in production code.
Example
If observed ranges match a particle's expected ranges within sigma = 0.2 m, that particle receives high weight and will likely survive resampling.
Pitfall
Multiplying many small probabilities causes underflow. Prefer summing log-likelihoods and exponentiating after normalization.
Practical tips
  • Normalize weights so they sum to one after the update.
  • Clip tiny weights to avoid numerical issues.
  • Consider beam subsampling or precomputed ray tables for speed.
Key Takeaway

Accurate expected-measurement prediction and stable likelihood computation are essential to good particle weighting and subsequent resampling.

screens.title: Resampling: Concentrate on Likely Hypotheses
screens.narratorSegment: Resampling draws a new set of particles from the current weighted set, with probability proportional to weight. The intuition is simple: duplicate particles that explain sensors well, and discard unlikely ones. Systematic resampling is efficient and easy to implement: construct the cumulative weight distribution, pick a random offset in the uniform step, and sweep to select indices. After resampling, all particles have equal weight, because the sampling process encodes the posterior. A typical MATLAB implementation normalizes weights, computes the cumulative sum, then selects particles with replacement using the systematic rule. Be mindful of two practical effects: resampling combats degeneracy by refocusing particles, but it can also cause particle impoverishment because duplicated particles reduce diversity. That loss makes the filter brittle if the true state moves away from the dominated hypothesis. Use adaptive resampling — only resample when the effective number of particles falls below a threshold — to reduce unnecessary loss of diversity. Visualize the before-and-after particle cloud to verify the intended behavior. In practical terms, systematic resampling and why resampling resets weights. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Resampling selects particles proportional to weight and then resets weights, trading representation fidelity for concentration on plausible regions.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.3 › Resampling
Resampling

Systematic resampling and its trade-offs

Resampling concentrates particles in high-likelihood regions by sampling indices proportional to normalized weights, then resetting weights to uniform. Systematic resampling is commonly used for its simplicity and low variance.

MATLAB-style systematic resampling (illustrative)
weights = [particles.weight];
weights = weights / sum(weights);
cum = cumsum(weights);
new_particles = [];
step = 1 / num_particles;
start = rand() * step;
for i = 1:num_particles
    idx = find(cum >= start + (i-1)*step, 1);
    new_particles(i) = particles(idx);
    new_particles(i).weight = 1 / num_particles;
end
particles = new_particles;
Inspect weight histograms before resampling to detect degeneracy.
Example
A few high-weight particles are duplicated, producing clusters that reflect strong sensor evidence.
Common mistake
Resampling every timestep even when weights are already fairly uniform, causing unnecessary diversity loss.
When to resample
Compute the effective number of particles Neff = 1 / sum(w_i^2). Resample only when Neff drops below a chosen threshold, for example 0.5 * num_particles.
Key Takeaway

Use adaptive resampling triggered by Neff to balance focusing on likely hypotheses and preserving particle diversity.

screens.title: Degeneracy and Impoverishment
screens.narratorSegment: Particle degeneracy occurs when, after a few iterations, most particle weights are near zero and only a handful carry significant probability mass. This situation means the filter is effectively using only a few samples to represent the posterior, which reduces approximation quality and makes the filter vulnerable to unexpected state changes. Resampling reduces degeneracy by eliminating low-weight particles, but repeated resampling without introducing variation causes particle impoverishment: duplicated particles reduce diversity and limit the ability to track changes. Several strategies mitigate these issues. Adaptive resampling delays resampling until the effective number of particles is low. Regularization adds small random perturbations to particles after resampling to reintroduce diversity. Rao-Blackwellized particle filters reduce particle dimensionality by using analytic updates (Kalman filters) for linear subspaces and particles for the nonlinear part, improving sample efficiency. Another practical technique is random particle injection during suspected kidnapping events to allow recovery. Monitor diagnostics and visualize weight histograms: early detection of degeneracy lets you choose the right mitigation before failure. In practical terms, why particles collapse and how to preserve diversity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.3 › Degeneracy & Impoverishment
Problem

Degeneracy and impoverishment explained

Degeneracy: a few particles dominate weights. Impoverishment: resampling duplicates these particles and reduces diversity. Both harm long-term tracking ability.

Mitigation strategies
  • Adaptive resampling based on Neff threshold.
  • Regularization: add small noise after resampling.
  • Rao-Blackwellization to reduce particle dimensionality.
  • Random particle injection for kidnapped recovery.
Concrete example
If Neff falls below 0.3*N, resample and add Gaussian jitter with small sigma to each duplicated particle to restore spread.
Key Takeaway

Monitor Neff and use regularization or Rao-Blackwellization to keep the filter robust without excessive particle counts.

Quick comparison
Degeneracy
Most particles have negligible weight; representation poor.
Impoverishment
Loss of hypothesis diversity after repeated resampling.

screens.narratorSegment: Adaptive resampling uses the effective number of particles, Neff, as a trigger. Neff compactly measures weight concentration: Neff equals one over the sum of squared normalized weights. If weights are uniform, Neff equals the total number of particles; if a single particle has all the weight, Neff is one. Set a threshold such as 0.5 times the particle count and only resample when Neff falls below that threshold. This reduces unnecessary resampling and preserves diversity when weights are well distributed. Implement Neff efficiently by normalizing weights then computing the reciprocal of the sum of squares. After computing Neff, branch: if Neff < threshold, execute systematic resampling and optionally regularize; otherwise skip resampling this timestep. Skipping resampling preserves unique samples and can slow the growth of impoverishment. A final tip: report Neff during simulation logs and use it to tune your resampling threshold empirically for a given map and sensor model. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.3 › Adaptive Resampling
Adaptive strategy

Effective number of particles guides resampling

Compute Neff and resample only when it falls below a threshold. This keeps resampling from needlessly reducing diversity.

Formula
Neff = 1 / sum(w_i^2) where weights are normalized so sum(w_i)=1.
Procedure
  1. Normalize weights.
  2. Compute Neff.
  3. If Neff < threshold, resample and optionally regularize.
  4. Otherwise, keep current set and proceed.
Key Takeaway

Neff provides a simple, interpretable trigger for resampling that mitigates unnecessary loss of particle diversity.

Tuning tips
  • Start with threshold = 0.5 * N and tune based on Neff traces.
  • Lower thresholds reduce resampling frequency but risk degeneracy.
  • Report Neff per timestep in simulation to guide parameter selection.

screens.title: Rao-Blackwellized Particle Filters
screens.narratorSegment: Rao-Blackwellized particle filters split the state into parts that are efficiently handled analytically and parts that require sampling. The canonical case is a robot with a linear-Gaussian substructure: use Kalman filters to maintain conditional distributions for those linear components and particles for the remaining nonlinear variables. This decomposition reduces the dimensionality of the particle space and improves sample efficiency because each particle carries a local analytic belief for the tractable subspace. In practice, construct particles for the nonlinear variables and attach a small Kalman filter instance to each particle for the linear variables. During the update phase, compute the Kalman update conditioned on the particle hypothesis, then weight the particle by the marginal likelihood. Rao-Blackwellization reduces the number of particles needed for accurate approximation and can dramatically lower computational cost in mixed systems. A key caveat is model correctness: identify the linear part correctly and ensure conditional independence assumptions hold. When applicable, this hybrid method often outperforms pure sampling approaches in both accuracy and speed. Rao-Blackwellized Particle Filters means use analytic kalman updates for linear subspaces and particles for the nonlinear parts to improve efficiency and accuracy.. In practical terms, hybrid approach: particles for nonlinear parts, kalman filters for linear parts. Architecture

Mix analytic and sampling updates

Factor the state into linear and nonlinear components. Use Kalman updates for the linear part per particle, reducing the dimension that particles must explore.

Each particle contains a hypothesis for the nonlinear variables and a small Kalman filter for the conditional linear variables.
Benefit

When a portion of your state is linear-Gaussian, Rao-Blackwellization reduces particle dimensionality and improves efficiency.

When to use
Use this hybrid when the system decomposes naturally and analytic updates exist for a conditional subset of variables. It is more complex but often worth the overhead.

screens.title: Monte Carlo Localization (MCL) and Kidnapping Recovery
screens.narratorSegment: Monte Carlo Localization applies the particle filter specifically to robot pose estimation in a known map. Start by uniformly sampling particles across free space to encode complete uncertainty. Then iterate prediction, sensor update, and resampling. Over time, particles concentrate around the true pose. An important real-world test is the kidnapped robot: the robot is moved without warning to a new location. A naive particle filter may fail because all particles are near the old pose. A robust approach injects a fraction of random particles uniformly across the map at each resampling step or when a divergence criterion is met. This random injection allows the filter to rediscover the true pose if sufficient particles happen to land near it. KLD-sampling and other adaptive particle number schemes adjust the particle count to guarantee a given approximation quality and can also help recovery. When visualizing MCL, watch for gradual convergence from uniform clouds to tight clusters, then watch how injection helps the cloud reseed after a kidnapping event. These behaviors are essential for safe deployment in dynamic environments. Monte Carlo Localization (MCL) and Kidnapping Recovery means mcl initializes particles across the map, iterates predict-update-resample, and uses random injection to recover from kidnapping events.. In practical terms, applying particle filters on a known map and recovering from teleportation. Module 7 › Chapter 6.3 › MCL & Kidnapping Recovery
Monte Carlo Localization

Run MCL on a known map and handle kidnapping

Start with uniform particles across free space. Iterate predict, update, resample. Use random particle injection to enable recovery from sudden relocations.

Kidnapping strategy
At each resample, optionally replace a small fraction of particles with uniformly sampled ones. If sensor mismatch is detected, increase injection temporarily.
Visualization practice

Random particle injection is a simple and effective tool to let MCL recover after unexpected teleportation of the robot.

  • Start with 1000 particles on a 20×20 grid as in the lab.

Module 7 › Chapter 6.3 › MATLAB Implementation
Starter structure

Organize code into modular functions for clarity and easier debugging. Keep the top-level loop short and readable.

Top-level pseudocode
function particles = mcl_localize(particles, map, odometry, measurement)
    particles = motion_update(particles, odometry);
    particles = sensor_update(particles, map, measurement);
    particles = resample(particles);
end
Visualization
Plot particles as small blue markers, true pose as red, and estimated mean as green. Update the plot each timestep to watch convergence.
Kidnapping test
At step 50 set the true pose to a random free-space location and observe whether the filter recovers with or without random particle injection.
Simulation parameters
  • Grid: 20×20 with several rectangular obstacles.
  • Particles: 1000 initial samples across free space.
  • Noise: odometry sigma 0.1 m; range sigma 0.2 m.
  • Steps: 100 timesteps; kidnap at step 50.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why particle filters exist, how they represent belief with particles, and when they outperform classic Gaussian estimators. We start from the practical problem: a robot that does not know where it is, or that sees ambiguous places that produce two or more plausible locations. Kalman-style filters assume a single Gaussian hypothesis and will collapse multimodal possibilities into one average that is often wrong. Particle filters solve this by representing the full distribution with many sampled hypotheses called particles. You will see the three core algorithmic moves: prediction using a motion model plus noise, update using sensor likelihoods, and resampling to focus computation on plausible areas. I will also highlight failure modes — degeneracy and impoverishment — and common practical fixes like adaptive resampling and random particle injection for kidnapped-robot recovery. By the end you will understand when to choose a particle filter, the basic MATLAB structure for implementing Monte Carlo Localization, and the concrete visualization you can use to debug and teach this approach.

These objectives orient our work with particle filters. First, you will explain the Monte Carlo method as a sampling-based approximate inference technique and why sampling approximates arbitrary distributions. Second, you will implement a particle filter for robot localization in a known map, including motion update, sensor likelihood, and systematic resampling in code. Third, you will understand and diagnose particle degeneracy: why particle weights collapse and how resampling both helps and hurts by causing impoverishment. Fourth, you will compare particle filters to Kalman-style estimators and decide which approach fits a localization scenario. Each objective is paired with a small mnemonic or visual to help you recall the skill: sampling landscapes, code blocks, diversity gauges, and comparison tables. These objectives prepare you to build, test, and evaluate Monte Carlo Localization in simulation and to reason about trade-offs when deploying on real robots.

We will translate theory into practice through a MATLAB-based hands-on activity. You will initialize a thousand particles uniformly across free space and simulate noisy odometry and range readings. You will visualize the particle cloud as blue points, the true robot pose as a red point, and the particle mean as a green point. You will perform a kidnapping experiment: at a chosen step, teleport the robot to a new location and observe whether the filter recovers. You will try remedies such as injecting random particles and applying regularization noise after resampling. These exercises train you to recognize failure modes and tune parameters: number of particles, sensor noise sigma, and resampling threshold. By the end, you will not only run the filter but also interpret the visualization to debug errors and choose appropriate mitigation strategies.

Begin by clarifying a common misconception: Kalman filters are not wrong, they are specialized. A Kalman filter represents the robot state as a single Gaussian distribution. That is ideal when motion and measurement noise are approximately Gaussian and the posterior remains unimodal. But many realistic localization problems are multimodal or non-Gaussian. For example, at startup the robot's pose prior is uniform; the robot could be anywhere on the map. Later, ambiguous environments create multiple equally plausible poses — two identical corridors produce a bimodal posterior. A Kalman filter collapses these modes into a single average, which often sits between the true hypotheses and produces meaningless estimates. Particle filters, by contrast, represent the full posterior with samples and naturally express multimodality. A key practical check is to visualize the belief: if your distribution has separated clusters, a sampling approach is required. Remember a common trap: adding process noise to an EKF does not create multiple peaks. It only broadens a single mode. The takeaway is clear: use Kalman methods for well-localized, approximately Gaussian scenarios and use particle methods when the belief can split or when sensors produce non-Gaussian uncertainty.

A particle is simply a sampled hypothesis of the robot's full state, typically pose in 2D: x, y, and heading. Collectively, particles form a non-parametric approximation to the posterior distribution. The key idea is density: regions with many particles represent high posterior probability. This representation is flexible: it handles uniform priors, multimodal posteriors, and arbitrary noise models. Practically, implement particles as a list of structs or arrays with fields for pose and weight. Sampling uniformly across free space creates a uniform prior. As the robot moves and senses, particles migrate and reweight, forming clusters around likely locations. An important practical point is memory and compute scaling: the number of particles needed typically grows with state complexity, and each particle may require an expensive sensor prediction such as ray casting. Visual inspection is an invaluable debugging tool: plot particles as blue dots, and show the weighted mean as an estimate. Also compute diagnostic statistics such as variance and effective particle number. A useful heuristic is to begin with a few hundred to a few thousand particles and adjust based on map complexity and available C P U. What matters is that the particle set remains diverse enough to represent plausible alternatives.

The prediction step moves each particle according to the robot's motion model plus process noise. This models uncertainty in control and odometry. Implementing this is straightforward conceptually: add the commanded displacement to each particle's pose and then add random noise sampled from the motion noise distribution. In MATLAB, a loop over particles updates x, y, and theta by delta values plus noise terms drawn per particle. Important practical notes: apply motion in the particle's local frame if the motion model is odometry-based, and ensure angular wrapping for theta. Use vectorized operations when possible to speed up MATLAB code. Too little motion noise will prevent particles from covering the true posterior after uncertain moves; too much noise will scatter particles and reduce weight concentration. For example, if odometry sigma is 0.1 meters per step, sample additive Gaussian noise per particle with that sigma. Finally, keep the prediction code separate from the sensor update to simplify testing and debugging. Prediction Step (Motion Update) means move particles with the motion model and add realistic process noise; vectorize updates for performance.. In practical terms, propagating particles with the motion model and process noise. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The update step weights each particle by the likelihood of the observed sensor measurement given the particle's pose. For range sensors, compute expected ranges using ray casting from the particle pose into the known map. Then evaluate a Gaussian likelihood for each beam: the closer the expected range to the observed range, the higher the likelihood. Multiply beam likelihoods to get the particle weight, or sum log-likelihoods to avoid numerical underflow. Practical tips: normalize weights to sum to one, clamp extremely small weights, and use log-space for many beams. If your sensor has non-Gaussian characteristics, adapt the likelihood model accordingly. A common optimization is to subsample beams or precompute ray-cast tables for faster expected-range queries. Also watch for correlated beams: multiplying many nearly redundant likelihoods can overconstrain the weights. After updating, inspect the weight distribution: if nearly all weight is on a few particles, degeneracy is imminent and resampling may be required. Finally, remember to keep weights non-negative and reset them after resampling. Update Step (Sensor Likelihoods) means weight particles by sensor likelihoods derived from expected measurements; normalize and monitor weight concentration to detect degeneracy.. In practical terms, compute how well each particle explains the sensor observation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Resampling draws a new set of particles from the current weighted set, with probability proportional to weight. The intuition is simple: duplicate particles that explain sensors well, and discard unlikely ones. Systematic resampling is efficient and easy to implement: construct the cumulative weight distribution, pick a random offset in the uniform step, and sweep to select indices. After resampling, all particles have equal weight, because the sampling process encodes the posterior. A typical MATLAB implementation normalizes weights, computes the cumulative sum, then selects particles with replacement using the systematic rule. Be mindful of two practical effects: resampling combats degeneracy by refocusing particles, but it can also cause particle impoverishment because duplicated particles reduce diversity. That loss makes the filter brittle if the true state moves away from the dominated hypothesis. Use adaptive resampling — only resample when the effective number of particles falls below a threshold — to reduce unnecessary loss of diversity. Visualize the before-and-after particle cloud to verify the intended behavior. Resampling: Concentrate on Likely Hypotheses means resampling selects particles proportional to weight and then resets weights, trading representation fidelity for concentration on plausible regions.. In practical terms, systematic resampling and why resampling resets weights. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Particle degeneracy occurs when, after a few iterations, most particle weights are near zero and only a handful carry significant probability mass. This situation means the filter is effectively using only a few samples to represent the posterior, which reduces approximation quality and makes the filter vulnerable to unexpected state changes. Resampling reduces degeneracy by eliminating low-weight particles, but repeated resampling without introducing variation causes particle impoverishment: duplicated particles reduce diversity and limit the ability to track changes. Several strategies mitigate these issues. Adaptive resampling delays resampling until the effective number of particles is low. Regularization adds small random perturbations to particles after resampling to reintroduce diversity. Rao-Blackwellized particle filters reduce particle dimensionality by using analytic updates (Kalman filters) for linear subspaces and particles for the nonlinear part, improving sample efficiency. Another practical technique is random particle injection during suspected kidnapping events to allow recovery. Monitor diagnostics and visualize weight histograms: early detection of degeneracy lets you choose the right mitigation before failure. Degeneracy and Impoverishment means degeneracy concentrates weight on few particles; resampling can cause impoverishment. use adaptive strategies and regularization to keep diversity.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Adaptive resampling uses the effective number of particles, Neff, as a trigger. Neff compactly measures weight concentration: Neff equals one over the sum of squared normalized weights. If weights are uniform, Neff equals the total number of particles; if a single particle has all the weight, Neff is one. Set a threshold such as 0.5 times the particle count and only resample when Neff falls below that threshold. This reduces unnecessary resampling and preserves diversity when weights are well distributed. Implement Neff efficiently by normalizing weights then computing the reciprocal of the sum of squares. After computing Neff, branch: if Neff < threshold, execute systematic resampling and optionally regularize; otherwise skip resampling this timestep. Monte Carlo Localization applies the particle filter specifically to robot pose estimation in a known map. Start by uniformly sampling particles across free space to encode complete uncertainty.
